title: Stones and candles
hookLine: a stone left on a grave, and a candle each year on the yahrzeit

cards: A Jewish cemetery on a weekday afternoon. No funeral. Just rows of headstones, and on top of some, small stones: a gray pebble, a chip of granite, a smooth one carried from a beach in someone's pocket.

Nobody sells them at the gate. People bring them, or bend down and pick one up from the path. And across town, on a kitchen counter, a candle in a glass burns through an ordinary day, and nobody blows it out.
Two small objects finish the life cycle.

teach.b: First, the stone. There's no single agreed reason; people give several. Flowers wilt, and a stone doesn't.

A stone tells the family someone came, even if nobody saw. And behind it is an old picture: in Genesis, when Rachel dies on the road, "Jacob set up a pillar upon her grave." She was here, and she was loved.
Second, the candle, which you met near the end of year three. Each year, on the anniversary of a death by the Hebrew calendar, families mark the yahrzeit, a Yiddish word for that day.
A candle is lit at home and left to burn through the day. People often connect it to Proverbs: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." A small flame for a whole life.
Third, what goes with it. On the yahrzeit, children say Kaddish for a parent, and some give to charity or study a little Torah in their memory.
The dead are remembered by the living doing good. Fourth, the whole block.

teach.h: THE LIFE CYCLE, LOOKED BACK ON.
teach.b: It began with the idea that a life has rituals. A baby welcomed at the door, a covenant, a daughter's name, a first haircut, honey on the letters. Coming of age.
A match, a canopy, seven blessings, a broken glass, peace in the home. Then the holy society, plain wood, the tear, the shovel, seven days, thirty days. And now a pebble and a flame.
From the first welcome to the last stone, nobody passes through a Jewish life alone.

how: Jewish visitors to a grave often leave a small stone on the headstone, and each year on the yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death, families light a memorial candle at home, and children say Kaddish for a parent.

o: gifts placed in a coffin before the burial
a pebble left on a grave and a yearly memorial flame
lights and gravel used to mark a holy boundary

games.q: stones and candles — tap the pairs.
p: the yearly anniversary of a death
set up a pillar on Rachel's grave
the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD

s: there is one official reason for leaving stones on Jewish graves
people give several: stones don't wilt, they show someone came, they echo old grave markers.
the yahrzeit is marked by the Hebrew calendar
the anniversary of the death is counted by the Hebrew date.
the yahrzeit candle is lit once and blown out after a few minutes
it's left to burn through the day.

games.q: you're visiting a Jewish grave for the first time and want to leave something. what is the custom?
o: a small stone on the headstone.
a lit candle on the grave.
games.why: a small stone. it doesn't wilt, and it tells the family that someone came.

practice: Hold a stone or pebble if one is near, or picture one, and feel its weight and its edges.
Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you knew or have only heard about, and let the stone stand for one thing you remember about them; if you pray, remember them in your prayer.
And if missing someone ever feels like too much to carry, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Stones and candles. A pebble left on a grave to say someone came, and a flame each year on the yahrzeit. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a lamp or candle, the word in Proverbs' line about the human spirit.

carryVoice: Your line: stones remember. Someone came, and someone still remembers. That closes the life cycle.
